The Campanella family purchased the restaurant from a court-appointed receiver several months ago and is preparing the dining room and kitchen for a grand reopening. The return restores a familiar local name and puts the business back under family ownership.

The restaurant entered receivership after a business dispute and fraud allegations involving Andrew Loffredo in May. Those claims are allegations, and this report does not treat them as proven. The receivership provided the legal process through which the property and operating assets could be transferred.

Owners announced the reopening date Monday. Details such as regular hours, reservations and the full opening menu may be updated closer to September 16, so customers should check the restaurant’s official channels before visiting. The confirmed development is that the family completed the purchase and has set a public date to resume service.
dek: The longtime restaurant is preparing to welcome customers back after the Campanella family purchased it from a court-appointed receiver.
headline: Campanella’s in Cranston plans September 16 reopening

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Wolfeboro selectmen have rejected demolition of the Libby Museum and agreed to pursue a path that could place the historic building under new stewardship.

The vote followed two public hearings in August where residents strongly supported preserving the structure. Board members also agreed to seek a meeting with the New Hampshire Attorney General’s Charitable Trusts Unit and local preservation groups to map out the required legal process.

A newly formed Libby Museum Preservation Society wants to become the successor trustee through Carroll County Probate Court and use private funding to restore or rebuild the property while continuing its natural-history mission. The museum opened in 1912 and its building has been closed since 2024 because of mold, structural deterioration and deferred maintenance.

The decision keeps the building standing, but it does not by itself reopen the museum or settle who will manage it. Officials still must address the collection, restoration costs and court approvals. The board’s immediate action removes demolition as the preferred option and creates room for a preservation plan.
dek: The board voted to keep the historic natural-history museum standing and begin work toward new stewardship after strong public support for preservation.
headline: Wolfeboro selectmen reject demolition of Libby Museum

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Fall color in New Hampshire’s White Mountains may arrive later than usual but last longer, according to regional foliage forecasters interviewed by the Conway Daily Sun.

Forecasters pointed to healthy, full canopies and improved moisture after earlier drought conditions as reasons for optimism. They expect color to progress by elevation from late September into the middle of October rather than peak everywhere at once.

The outlook remains weather-dependent. Warm sunny days followed by crisp nights can help leaves produce vivid reds and oranges, while a hurricane, severe storm or strong wind event could remove leaves before peak color. Daylight loss, temperature and moisture all influence the timing.

For visitors and tourism businesses, a longer progression can spread travel across several weekends. Routes through the Kancamagus Scenic Highway, Pinkham Notch, Franconia and Kinsman Notch are among the areas expected to draw foliage traffic. The forecast is not a guarantee; travelers should check current foliage maps and local conditions before choosing a destination.
dek: Healthy canopies and improved moisture conditions could support bright color from late September into mid-October, depending on elevation and weather.
headline: White Mountains forecasters expect later, longer foliage season

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Three jurors from Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial have described the deliberations that ended in a mistrial, offering a new account of the panel’s internal deadlock.

The jury foreperson and two other panelists told NBC10 Boston that one juror would not join the rest of the panel in a verdict. They said deliberations became tense and that several jurors changed their views while reviewing the evidence and competing arguments about criminal responsibility.

Their interview reflects the recollections of three jurors, not a formal court finding about every member of the panel. NBC10 Boston said it tried to contact the juror described by the others as the holdout.

A judge declared the mistrial last week after the jury reported it could not reach a unanimous decision. The case remains unresolved, and prosecutors and the court must determine the next procedural steps. Nothing said after the mistrial changes the presumption of innocence or constitutes a verdict. The interview is significant because it adds firsthand context to the note and courtroom discussions that preceded the judge’s decision.
dek: The jury foreperson and two other panelists told NBC10 Boston that one holdout prevented agreement in the closely watched murder case.
headline: Three Lindsay Clancy jurors describe deadlock after mistrial

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Four people were injured in a two-car rear-end crash on Route 9 in Framingham Sunday night, according to police information reported by Patch and NBC10 Boston.

The collision happened around 8:25 p.m. near 1063 Worcester Road. One injured person was flown by medical helicopter to Boston Medical Center, while three others were taken by ambulance to MetroWest Medical Center.
Officials had not released the names of the people involved or updates on their medical conditions in the latest report. Police also had not announced a preliminary cause, citations or charges.

The investigation remains open. The use of a medical helicopter indicates the urgency of the response but does not establish a patient’s final diagnosis or prognosis. Drivers who witnessed the collision or recorded the area on a dashboard camera can contact Framingham police through the department’s regular channels. Until investigators issue findings, details such as speed, distraction or impairment should not be assumed.
dek: One person was flown to Boston Medical Center and three others went to MetroWest Medical Center after the Sunday-night collision.
headline: Four injured in Framingham Route 9 rear-end crash

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A 26-year-old Providence woman faces charges after a hit-and-run in Pawtucket left a man critically injured, police said.

Authorities allege that Maryna Ohagan was driving a vehicle reported stolen earlier Sunday when it struck a 48-year-old man on an electric unicycle at Main and Magill streets. The injured man was taken to a hospital with life-threatening injuries.

Pawtucket police said officers had briefly pursued the vehicle after trying to stop it but ended the chase for public-safety reasons. Investigators allege the driver fled on foot after the collision. Providence police later arrested Ohagan, and Pawtucket police said she admitted involvement in the theft and crash.

Ohagan faces charges including possession of a stolen vehicle, reckless driving, leaving a crash that caused serious injury and larceny over $10,000. The charges are allegations and have not been proved in court. She is presumed innocent unless convicted, and officials have not released a later update on the victim’s condition.
dek: Police say a stolen vehicle struck a 48-year-old man riding an electric unicycle, leaving him with life-threatening injuries.
headline: Providence woman charged after Pawtucket hit-and-run

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Bus riders and transportation advocates are pressing Rhode Island officials to keep RIPTA’s main Providence hub at Kennedy Plaza.

The Kennedy Plaza Resilience Coalition scheduled a Tuesday evening rally to oppose proposals that would move the terminal closer to the Amtrak station. Similar relocation ideas have circulated for years as state and city leaders consider changes to downtown transportation.

The coalition argues that moving the hub would spend public money while making downtown access harder for seniors and riders with disabilities. Supporters of a relocation have described potential connections among bus, rail and development projects, but the cited report did not identify a newly approved site or final construction plan.

The dispute remains a planning debate rather than a completed move. Any relocation would require public decisions on design, funding, accessibility and service patterns. Kennedy Plaza currently functions as a central transfer point, so riders are focused on whether a new location would preserve practical connections to jobs, services and other bus routes.
dek: A Providence coalition organized a rally opposing proposals to move the downtown bus terminal near the Amtrak station.
headline: Riders press to keep RIPTA hub at Kennedy Plaza

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: North Korea has built a new uranium-enrichment facility at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex, the International Atomic Energy Agency said in a report disclosed Wednesday.

The agency assessed that the two-story building could hold as many as 28 centrifuge cascades. It also reported expanded operations at an annex of the Kangson enrichment site near Pyongyang, pointing to growth in nuclear infrastructure at more than one location.

IAEA inspectors have not had access to North Korea since 2009. The agency said its assessment relies on satellite imagery and other open-source material, including photographs released by North Korean state media after a June visit by leader Kim Jong Un.

The findings do not provide a public measurement of current enriched-uranium output. They document new capacity and operating indicators that the agency considers serious. North Korea says its nuclear status is irreversible and disputes the IAEA’s authority over its program. Additional imagery or official disclosures may refine the assessment, making the development subject to continued monitoring.
dek: The nuclear watchdog says a two-story building at Yongbyon could hold up to 28 centrifuge cascades as infrastructure expands at multiple sites.
headline: IAEA reports new North Korea uranium-enrichment facility

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Ukraine is contracting for roughly 1,000 Patriot air-defense missiles with allied help and financing tied to a European Union loan, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said.

Khmara told a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group that most of the missiles would arrive over several years. He asked partner countries to provide interceptors from existing stockpiles now, arguing that immediate defenses are needed against continuing Russian missile and drone attacks.

Germany separately said it would urgently supply additional Patriot PAC-2 interceptors from its own stocks and expand deliveries of other air-defense equipment. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte urged members to increase support.

The contracts represent planned supply, not 1,000 missiles already delivered or available for use. Timing, participating suppliers and annual delivery volumes were not fully detailed in the initial report. Ukraine also identified a major financing gap for drone purchases. The story remains developing because allied commitments, production schedules and near-term transfers will determine how quickly the announced plan strengthens air defenses.
dek: Kyiv’s defense chief says most deliveries will take years and is asking allies to release interceptors from existing stocks sooner.
headline: Ukraine contracts for about 1,000 Patriot missiles

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Chinese artificial-intelligence startup DeepSeek has selected CITIC Securities to prepare for a domestic initial public offering, according to two people familiar with the matter cited by Reuters.

The company is working toward a possible listing on Shanghai’s technology-focused STAR Market. Selecting an adviser and beginning pre-listing preparation moves the process forward, but it is not the same as filing a final prospectus or setting an offer date.

DeepSeek became a prominent competitor in generative AI by developing models designed to use computing resources efficiently. A public listing could provide additional capital for computing infrastructure, model development and hiring as competition for researchers and hardware intensifies.

Important terms remain unsettled, including timing, valuation and the amount of stock to be sold. DeepSeek and CITIC Securities had not publicly confirmed a final transaction in the initial report. Any eventual offering would also require regulatory review. The current development is therefore a preparatory step, not a completed IPO or a publicly traded share price.
dek: Sources say the Chinese AI startup has selected the brokerage for work ahead of a possible STAR Market listing, though final terms remain undecided.
headline: DeepSeek taps CITIC Securities for Shanghai IPO preparations

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Indian space startup GalaxEye has received a U.S. patent for satellite-imaging technology that synchronizes optical and radar sensors.

The system is designed to capture both types of data at the same time and location. Optical cameras can produce familiar, detailed images but are limited by darkness and clouds, while radar can operate at night and through many weather conditions. Combining them can make Earth-observation data more consistent.

GalaxEye says possible uses include disaster response, agriculture, insurance and security. The company, founded by engineers from the Indian Institute of Technology Madras, has raised about $21 million and plans a constellation of 30 satellites over five years. It also acquired Bengaluru spacecraft-engineering company StarOps.

A patent protects the covered invention in the United States but does not by itself prove commercial adoption or performance at constellation scale. GalaxEye still must build, launch and operate the planned satellites. The award is nevertheless a concrete step as private space companies compete to deliver more frequent and weather-resilient imagery.
dek: The Indian space startup says its technology synchronizes two sensor types to capture more consistent Earth-observation data through darkness and clouds.
headline: GalaxEye wins U.S. patent for combined radar-optical satellite imaging

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The Japanese yen’s advance toward a seven-month high is putting renewed pressure on a long-running strategy used across global markets: the yen carry trade.

In a carry trade, investors borrow in a currency with relatively low interest rates and invest the proceeds in higher-yielding currencies or assets. The approach benefited from Japan’s years of very easy monetary policy, especially when U.S. rates rose sharply in 2022 and 2023.

That advantage can shrink when the yen strengthens or Japanese borrowing costs rise. Markets now expect the Bank of Japan may tighten policy, raising the risk that investors must unwind leveraged positions. Reuters reported yen-based cross-border borrowing reached a record 360 trillion yen in March, though the full size of carry trades is difficult to measure.

The current adjustment appears more anticipated than the abrupt 2024 unwind, but currency and rate moves can still transmit volatility across stocks, bonds and emerging markets. The figures describe reported positioning and delayed market conditions, not a live quote or investment recommendation.
dek: Expectations for Bank of Japan tightening are narrowing the advantage of borrowing cheaply in yen to buy higher-yielding assets.
headline: Stronger yen puts carry trade under renewed pressure

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Singapore Airlines plans to seek stronger governance rights and clearer loss-reduction commitments before agreeing to provide additional capital to Air India, according to sources cited by Reuters.

Air India has requested about $1.5 billion in new equity. Tata Sons, the controlling shareholder, has approved roughly $1.1 billion as its proportional contribution. Singapore Airlines owns 25.1% of the carrier but has not made a final decision on joining the funding round.

The Singapore carrier wants more influence over management and board oversight as it evaluates further exposure to Air India’s turnaround. Air India recorded a $2.33 billion loss in its last fiscal year, increasing scrutiny of the capital request.

Singapore Airlines said investment decisions would be made with its own resources; state investor Temasek would not directly fund the contribution. The talks concern potential financing and conditions, not a completed transaction. Amounts, governance terms and timing could change before any agreement. No share-price claim in this report is presented as live.
dek: Sources say the 25.1% shareholder wants greater governance influence and loss-reduction commitments before providing more capital.
headline: Singapore Airlines seeks stronger terms before new Air India funding

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The Rhode Island Lottery has launched Powerball Xs & Os, a football-themed draw game that uses NFL team logos rather than game scores.

Players choose eight logos from the league’s 32 teams. Eight winning logos will be drawn at random each Sunday at 10 p.m. beginning September 13. Matching at least four can produce a cash prize, while matching all eight wins a rolling jackpot that starts at $1 million.

The lottery emphasized that results are random and have no connection to NFL game outcomes. Tickets cost $5 and are available from Rhode Island Lottery retailers, RILot.com and the lottery’s mobile app.

Tickets can also generate entries for separate promotional drawings that may offer NFL merchandise, experiences or a Super Bowl trip. Those promotions do not change the underlying odds of the draw game. As with any lottery product, buying a ticket does not guarantee a return, and the announced jackpot is a prize pool rather than a prediction that someone will win in a particular week.
dek: The $5 game asks players to select eight team logos, with weekly drawings beginning September 13 and a rolling jackpot starting at $1 million.
headline: Rhode Island launches NFL-themed Powerball Xs & Os game

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A resident wish program at Mountain View Community in Ossipee helped 93-year-old Ruth Beckwith return to a New Hampshire lake with her family.

Beckwith, who uses a wheelchair and has difficulty getting into a car, visited Wentworth State Park in Wolfeboro on August 19. She entered Lake Wentworth using a water wheelchair rented from Northeast Passage, the adaptive-recreation program at the University of New Hampshire.

Family members, including several great-grandchildren, joined her for the outing. The visit fulfilled Beckwith’s request to swim in a lake one more time and required coordination among nursing-home staff, relatives and the equipment provider.

Mountain View Community is Carroll County’s nursing home. The trip illustrates how adaptive recreation can make an ordinary family experience accessible to someone with limited mobility. The event was not a medical treatment or public program announcement; it was a personalized outing organized around one resident’s goal. For Beckwith and her family, the result was a day together at the water.
dek: Mountain View Community arranged adaptive equipment so resident Ruth Beckwith could swim at Wentworth State Park with her family.
headline: Ossipee nursing-home program helps 93-year-old return to lake

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Fire departments and residents across southern New Hampshire gathered to honor Raymond firefighter Eric Phillips during a dignified transfer from Concord on Sunday.

Phillips, 44, died Friday night after suffering a medical emergency while responding to a call for service, according to reporting compiled by the Daily Dispatch from WMUR. The transfer began shortly after 4:30 p.m. in Concord, and more than a dozen departments took part in the procession.

Firefighters positioned apparatus on Route 101 overpasses as the procession traveled toward Raymond. Community members also stood along the route. The coordinated display followed a long emergency-services tradition of accompanying a fallen responder and visibly supporting the person’s family and department.

Phillips had served with the Raymond Fire Department for five years. The public observance brought together departments that routinely assist one another across town lines, especially during large fires and other emergencies. Officials had not announced additional public memorial arrangements in the source report. Residents should rely on the Raymond Fire Department or town notices for any later service information.
dek: More than a dozen departments joined a dignified transfer for Eric Phillips, who died after a medical emergency while responding to a call.
headline: New Hampshire fire departments honor fallen Raymond firefighter

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Dover will dedicate a new permanent 9/11 memorial Friday as the city marks 25 years since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

The remembrance ceremony is scheduled for 11 a.m. September 11 in the Cocheco Mill Courtyard on Central Avenue, according to a city announcement posted Tuesday. The dedication gives Dover a fixed public site for future remembrance in addition to this year’s anniversary program.

The timing places the local ceremony within a week of memorial events across New Hampshire and the country. Dover’s announcement centers its observance on both remembrance and the formal unveiling of the memorial rather than a temporary display.

Residents planning to attend should check the city’s event notice for any logistical updates before traveling downtown. The city had not described a weather alternative or changes to the 11 a.m. start in the posted notice. The event comes on a milestone anniversary when communities are also considering how to preserve firsthand memory for younger residents who were born after the attacks.
dek: The city plans an 11 a.m. remembrance ceremony Friday in the Cocheco Mill Courtyard, where its new memorial will be dedicated.
headline: Dover to dedicate permanent 9/11 memorial on 25th anniversary

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: One person suffered serious injuries in a collision involving a car and a bicycle in Medway on Tuesday night, authorities said.

Police and emergency crews responded on Milford Street near Clark Street. The injured person was taken to a hospital, according to Boston 25 News. Officials did not immediately release the person’s name, age or current condition.

Milford Street was closed in the area while first responders worked and police began their investigation. The initial report did not identify the driver, describe the direction of travel or say whether any citations or charges were being considered.

Because the available information remains preliminary, the cause of the crash and the sequence leading to impact are not yet established. Road users should avoid drawing conclusions until police release additional findings. The closure was announced as an active-scene measure; drivers should check Medway police updates for the road’s current status. Anyone who witnessed the collision or has relevant video should follow the department’s instructions if investigators request information.
dek: A car-and-bicycle crash Tuesday night sent one person to the hospital and temporarily closed part of Milford Street near Clark Street.
headline: Bicyclist seriously injured in Medway collision

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A judge has allowed attorneys for the family of Massachusetts State Trooper Kevin Trainor to attach a restaurant owner’s home and liquor license as security while their civil lawsuit proceeds.

The family is seeking $20 million from Tribu, a Saugus restaurant, after Trainor was killed in a wrong-way collision on Route 1 in May. Plaintiffs allege the driver was served nine drinks at the restaurant before leaving and striking Trainor’s vehicle. Those claims have not been resolved at trial.

At Tuesday’s Essex County Superior Court hearing, lawyers for the restaurant argued that the $20 million estimate was arbitrary and disputed whether the plaintiffs were likely to recover that amount. The judge nevertheless approved the requested attachments in place of insurance, Boston 25 News reported.

The decision does not determine liability or damages. It preserves identified assets while the parties begin discovery and litigate the underlying allegations. The Massachusetts Alcoholic Beverages Control Commission said it was still reviewing Tribu’s liquor license, which remained active at the time of the report.
dek: The ruling permits plaintiffs to attach a restaurant owner’s home and liquor license while a $20 million civil case moves into discovery.
headline: Judge allows asset attachments in Trooper Trainor family lawsuit

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Brown University and Brown University Health are launching an aging-research partnership backed by a $37 million investment from the Starr Foundation.

The Starr Healthspan Innovation Alliance is designed to move discoveries from university laboratories into clinical trials across the health system. Brown said the work will focus on age-associated diseases and on extending the years people remain healthy, rather than treating longevity as a single condition.

Funding will expand Brown’s Center on the Biology of Aging, support laboratory research and help recruit scientists in geroscience, the study of genetic, molecular and cellular mechanisms involved in aging. The health system’s clinical network is expected to provide a pathway for evaluating potential treatments with patients.

The alliance matters regionally because it connects a major Rhode Island research university with the state’s largest health system. Its announced aims include work relevant to cancer and dementia, but the partnership did not announce a specific new therapy or guarantee clinical outcomes. Individual studies will still require their own scientific review, trial design and patient-safety oversight.
dek: Brown University and Brown University Health will link laboratory work with clinical trials through a new Starr Foundation-backed partnership.
headline: Brown launches $37 million alliance for aging research

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Rhode Island vineyards are intensifying surveillance for spotted lanternflies as the invasive insect becomes established across all five counties.

The Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management says the species was first detected in Warwick in 2021, with the state’s first confirmed population identified near Route 7 in Smithfield the following year. Growers told NBC 10 they are working with RIDEM and University of Rhode Island researchers who regularly check monitoring traps.

Spotted lanternflies feed on sap from grapevines and other plants. Large infestations can weaken vines, reduce yields and leave plants more vulnerable to cold. Their sugary waste can also encourage sooty mold. Tree-of-heaven is a preferred host, so its presence near vineyards is one factor growers watch.

Researchers are studying possible controls, including a parasitoid that attacks lanternfly nymphs, but no biological-control agent is currently approved for release in Rhode Island. For now, early detection, reporting and removal of egg masses remain central tools. Residents should use RIDEM guidance before handling suspected insects or moving outdoor materials that may carry eggs.
dek: The invasive insect is established in all five counties, prompting vineyards and state researchers to expand monitoring of vines and nearby host trees.
headline: Spotted lanternfly spread puts Rhode Island vineyards on watch

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Iran’s Revolutionary Guard launched ballistic missiles toward a U.S. military base near Azraq, Jordan, and attacked ships in the Strait of Hormuz in a new escalation reported early Wednesday.

Reuters reported that Iran said it targeted 10 vessels, including two U.S. ships. Iranian authorities claimed damage at the Jordanian base, while Jordanian and U.S. officials reported no casualties and said most incoming missiles were intercepted. Independent confirmation of Iran’s damage claims was not immediately available.

The attacks followed the U.S. military’s destruction of five Iranian oil tankers, which Washington said was retaliation for strikes on an American warship. The exchange comes as fighting also threatens energy facilities and commercial shipping around the Gulf.

The Strait of Hormuz is a critical route for global oil exports, making any attack on vessels there consequential beyond the immediate military confrontation. Details about damage to the ships and the exact sequence of the attacks remained limited in the first report. This is a developing story, and casualty or damage assessments may change as governments and shipping operators release verified updates.
dek: Iran’s Revolutionary Guard launched missiles toward a U.S. base and said it struck 10 ships after American forces destroyed five Iranian tankers.
headline: Iran attacks U.S. base in Jordan and ships near Hormuz
location: Jordan and the Strait of Hormuz

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Indonesian rescuers are searching the Sunda Strait for eight people whose speedboat lost contact while traveling to Anak Krakatau to cover volcanic activity.

The group includes five photojournalists, two crew members and a route guide, the Associated Press reported. The boat departed Carita in Banten province, and relatives received its last known message at 6:13 p.m. Monday saying the group had reached waters near the island.

Their last reported position was about 18.5 kilometers, or roughly 11.5 miles, from shore. Search teams deployed Tuesday had not established contact or confirmed the boat’s location by early Wednesday. The journalists work for several Indonesian and international news organizations, with one described as a freelance photographer.

Anak Krakatau’s initial eruption ended Sunday, but the volcano has continued intermittent activity involving explosions, lava and ash. Officials had not established whether that activity, weather, mechanical failure or another cause was connected to the disappearance. The search remains active, and early details may change as rescue crews cover the area and review communications.
dek: A speedboat carrying five photojournalists, two crew members and a guide lost contact while traveling to report on the Indonesian volcano.
headline: Search underway for eight missing near Anak Krakatau

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: OpenAI says it is deepening work with Samsung Electronics on next-generation chips as the companies expand cooperation around artificial intelligence infrastructure and enterprise services.

Harrison Kim, general manager of OpenAI Korea, said at a Seoul press conference that the chip collaboration is making progress, Reuters reported. He did not provide technical specifications, a production timetable or financial terms, leaving the scope of the planned silicon unclear.

OpenAI has separately identified Samsung and SK Hynix as prospective memory suppliers for the Stargate data-center project through letters of intent. Advanced memory is a key constraint in AI systems because large models require chips that can move and store data at very high speeds.

OpenAI also said ChatGPT Enterprise usage in South Korea grew 28-fold over the past year and described Samsung as a major adopter across internal functions. Samsung declined to confirm customer-specific details in Reuters’ report. The announcement signals closer coordination, but it is not yet a product launch; manufacturing commitments, chip design and deployment milestones remain to be disclosed.
dek: OpenAI says the companies are advancing joint semiconductor work and expanding enterprise AI cooperation in South Korea.
headline: OpenAI and Samsung deepen work on next-generation chips

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Apple is scheduled to hold its fall product event Wednesday, the company’s first major launch presentation under chief executive John Ternus.

Reuters reported that Apple is expected to introduce its next iPhone lineup and may unveil a long-anticipated foldable model. The company had confirmed the September 9 event date but had not preannounced the devices, so product names, specifications and prices circulating before the presentation remain expectations rather than confirmed facts.

Ternus, Apple’s longtime hardware chief, became CEO September 1 as Tim Cook moved to executive chairman. That leadership change puts unusual attention on how the event frames Apple’s hardware priorities and its approach to artificial intelligence on consumer devices.

A foldable phone would place Apple in a segment already served by several rivals and could lift average selling prices, but demand will depend on durability, software and cost. The event itself will determine which reports were accurate. Customers considering an upgrade should wait for Apple’s published specifications and availability details rather than treating advance reports as final.
dek: The September 9 showcase is expected to introduce new iPhones and could offer the first public look at Apple’s next hardware strategy.
headline: Apple set for first major product event under new CEO

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Google plans to invest at least €13 billion, about $15.1 billion, in artificial-intelligence infrastructure in Finland over 2027 and 2028.

The company said the program will include new data centers, grid improvements, clean-energy projects and battery capacity, Reuters reported. Google described it as its largest single investment in Europe. Finland’s cold climate and relatively low-carbon electricity supply have made the country attractive for large computing facilities.

The commitment adds to a sharp rise in capital spending by major technology companies as they compete to secure electricity, land and specialized hardware for AI services. Alphabet has said its global spending could reach $195 billion to $205 billion, putting pressure on the company to show that higher infrastructure costs produce durable revenue growth.

The Finnish projects will unfold over multiple years, so the announced total is a planned commitment rather than money already spent. Construction schedules, permitting and energy availability can still affect timing. For investors, the development is another measure of how quickly AI competition is shifting from software releases toward long-lived physical assets.
dek: Alphabet’s Google says it will spend at least €13 billion over two years on data centers, power grids and supporting clean-energy projects.
headline: Google plans $15 billion AI infrastructure investment in Finland

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Amazon began selling its first sterling-denominated bonds Wednesday, opening a new currency market for the company as it finances heavy spending on artificial-intelligence infrastructure.

Lead managers were marketing four tranches with maturities of three, six, 12 and 19 years, Reuters reported. Initial price guidance ranged from about 70 basis points over comparable British government bonds for the shortest maturity to roughly 110 basis points for the longest.
Those spreads were preliminary indications, not final pricing. The deal was expected to be priced later Wednesday, and the eventual size and borrowing costs could change as investors submit orders.

Large technology companies have increasingly issued debt in currencies beyond the U.S. dollar, including euros, Swiss francs and yen. Doing so can broaden the investor base and match financing with global operations. Amazon’s sterling debut also illustrates the scale of capital needed for data centers, chips and network capacity. The transaction is a financing development, not a real-time signal about Amazon’s share price, and investors should use final deal documents for confirmed terms.
dek: The company began marketing four pound-denominated maturities as large technology firms diversify funding for heavy AI investment.
headline: Amazon enters sterling bond market for first time

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: London-based steakhouse Hawksmoor has opened a Boston location in Fort Point, giving the restaurant group its third U.S. outpost.

The new restaurant is on Necco Street and is led in the kitchen by Boston head chef Thomas Park, according to Axios Boston. Its core menu centers on dry-aged cuts, including porterhouse and rib chop sourced from Châtel Farms in Georgia.

The Boston location also adds references to the city’s food culture. Axios reported a pistachio espresso martini inspired by Caffè Vittoria and cream-filled chocolates offered in several flavors. Those details are intended to distinguish the restaurant from the company’s other U.S. locations rather than simply duplicate the London menu.

The opening adds another high-end dining option to Fort Point, a neighborhood where offices, housing and restaurants share former industrial blocks near the Seaport. Menu availability and prices can change after opening, so diners should check the restaurant’s current information before visiting. The launch is notable locally as another international hospitality brand tests a Boston-specific format.
dek: The London-born steakhouse has opened on Necco Street with a Boston-specific menu alongside its signature dry-aged steaks.
headline: Hawksmoor opens third U.S. restaurant in Boston’s Fort Point

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Boston’s post-Labor Day calendar moves from heavy metal to jazz, salsa and Caribbean carnival events over the next five days.

Iron Maiden is scheduled to bring its Run For Your Lives tour to TD Garden on Wednesday, September 9, with Megadeth on the bill, according to Axios Boston’s weekly events guide. On Thursday, Catherine Bent’s Antenna trio is due to perform at Long Live Roxbury from 6 to 9 p.m.

Saturday’s Embrace Massó ¡Con Salsa! Block Party is set for Summer Street Plaza from 3 to 7 p.m., headlined by El Gran Combo de Puerto Rico. The week closes Sunday with the 32nd Cambridge Carnival International in Central Square from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m.

The events vary in ticketing and admission, and schedules can change. Attendees should confirm details with each organizer before traveling, especially for outdoor programming. Taken together, the lineup highlights the range of regional cultural programming that resumes immediately after the holiday weekend, from arena touring acts to neighborhood-scale performances and public festivals.
dek: Iron Maiden, a Roxbury jazz trio, a free salsa block party and Cambridge Carnival anchor a busy post-Labor Day calendar.
headline: Boston week ahead spans metal, salsa and carnival

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Bow police searched Yihong Spa at 699 Route 3A on Tuesday as part of a months-long investigation into alleged human trafficking and prostitution-related offenses, according to the Concord Monitor.

Officers executed a search warrant at the business with assistance from the New Hampshire Attorney General’s Office and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. The report did not identify any arrests or charges resulting from the search.

Authorities had not publicly detailed how the investigation began, how many people may be involved or what evidence was collected. A search warrant authorizes investigators to look for specified evidence; it does not establish that a person or business committed a crime.

Bow Police Chief Ken Miller encouraged anyone with relevant information to contact the department. The case remains active, and additional details may emerge as investigators review material gathered during the search. Until authorities announce charges or court filings, allegations connected to the investigation remain unproven.
dek: Police executed a search warrant at a Route 3A spa after a months-long investigation, with state and federal agencies assisting.
headline: Bow spa searched in trafficking and prostitution investigation

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Concord City Manager Tom Aspell plans to retire January 31, ending more than two decades in the city’s top administrative job and just over 28 years at City Hall.

Aspell announced the decision Tuesday after returning from a six-week sabbatical, the Concord Monitor reported. He became interim city manager in 2005 and received the permanent appointment in 2006, after earlier roles in planning, economic development and as assistant city manager.

The retirement starts a significant leadership transition for New Hampshire’s capital. Concord is also dealing with a deputy city manager vacancy, leaving the City Council to decide how to structure and conduct a search while maintaining daily municipal operations.

Aspell arrived in Concord in 1998 after planning and economic-development work in Londonderry and Haverhill, Massachusetts. His January departure gives the council several months to outline a succession process. The city had not yet announced a permanent replacement or a detailed timetable for selecting one.
dek: The longtime city manager will step down January 31 after 21 years in the role and more than 28 years at City Hall.
headline: Concord city manager Tom Aspell to retire in January

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Somerville firefighters rescued a resident from a three-story apartment building after a fire broke out on Dartmouth Street shortly before 3 a.m. Monday, Boston 25 News reported.

Crews arrived to heavy flames on the first floor. A resident of that unit had already escaped by jumping and was treated for injuries described as not life-threatening. Firefighters then moved through heavy smoke to reach and remove a resident from the second floor.

Two cats were also rescued from the building. The report did not specify how many residents were displaced or provide an estimate of the property damage. Officials were continuing to investigate what started the fire.

The response closed off part of the neighborhood while crews worked inside the building and checked for remaining occupants. No firefighter injuries were reported in the initial account. Residents should rely on Somerville fire officials for any later findings about the cause, building access or assistance for people affected.
dek: Crews entered heavy smoke to remove a second-floor resident after another occupant escaped by jumping from the burning building.
headline: Somerville firefighters rescue resident from apartment blaze

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Stoughton officials decided Tuesday night to cancel the town’s contract with Flock Safety, the company whose automated license-plate reader cameras have drawn mounting privacy scrutiny across Massachusetts.

WCVB reported that residents raised concerns about the technology before the town acted. Flock systems capture vehicle plates and associated time and location information, data that police can search during investigations. The debate has centered on who may access those records, how long they are retained and how broadly they may be shared.

The Stoughton decision came as Quincy’s City Council considered the future of similar cameras but delayed its own decision. The two meetings show that communities are reaching different procedural stages while weighing public-safety claims against privacy and oversight questions.

WCVB’s initial report did not provide complete details on the timing for deactivation, equipment removal or any financial terms tied to Stoughton’s cancellation. Those implementation questions will determine how quickly data collection ends and whether town records remain available under existing retention rules.
dek: Town officials ended the license-plate reader agreement after residents raised privacy concerns, while Quincy delayed a separate decision.
headline: Stoughton ends Flock camera contract after privacy pushback

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The University of Rhode Island will hold its second annual Technology Showcase on September 22, bringing university researchers, startup founders, investors and industry representatives together in Kingston.

The event is scheduled for 4 to 7 p.m. at Toray Commons in the Fascitelli Center for Advanced Engineering. It is part of Rhode Island Startup Week and is designed to move research toward licensing, partnerships and new ventures.

URI said featured work will include smart-wound monitoring and PFAS detection. The university also pointed to recent commercialization activity: spinout Juice Robotics has licensed four URI technologies, Trace Sensing closed a seed round of more than $2 million and FastFlowLM joined an AMD program.

Those examples do not guarantee that every project at the showcase will attract funding or reach the market. They illustrate the event’s purpose: giving potential backers and partners an early look at applied research. Registration and the final program are available through URI, and schedule details may change before September 22.
dek: The September 22 event will put university inventions and startups in front of investors and industry partners during Rhode Island Startup Week.
headline: URI technology showcase will connect research with investors

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Rhode Island voters will cast primary ballots Wednesday, one day later than the state’s usual Tuesday schedule. Polling places across the state open at 7 a.m., except in New Shoreham, where voting begins at 9 a.m.
All polling places close at 8 p.m. The Secretary of State’s voter information site says anyone who is in line at their assigned polling location by 8 p.m. will still be allowed to vote.

The early-voting and emergency mail-ballot period ended Tuesday at 4 p.m. Voters can use the state’s online voter record tool to confirm their polling place and review election information before leaving home. Primary ballots select party nominees for federal, state and local offices.

The Wednesday election date was adopted because the previously scheduled Tuesday fell immediately after Labor Day. Election officials advise voters to verify their location rather than assume it is the same as in a prior election. Results will be reported after polls close; this article does not project any race.
dek: Most polling places open at 7 a.m. and close at 8 p.m. for the state’s unusually scheduled Wednesday primary.
headline: Rhode Island primary voting starts Wednesday morning

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A Ukrainian drone attack on the Russian Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk killed four people, including a child, regional Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said Wednesday.

Kondratyev said 29 people were injured, according to Reuters. The casualty figures and attribution came from Russian authorities and had not been independently verified in the initial report. Ukraine did not immediately provide a response in the account.

Novorossiysk is a major hub for Russian oil and grain exports, giving any attack there potential significance beyond the immediate damage. Early reporting did not establish whether port operations or export flows were disrupted.

The situation remains developing as local authorities assess damage and identify victims. Casualty totals can change after emergency crews complete searches and hospitals update patient conditions. Any claims about the target, the drones’ origin or the effect on shipping should be treated as preliminary until supported by additional evidence or official operational notices.
dek: Russian authorities reported four deaths and 29 injuries in an attack on the Black Sea city, a major oil and grain export hub.
headline: Four killed in drone attack on Russian port city, governor says

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Israel has told Britain to close its consulate in East Jerusalem within 30 days, according to Israeli officials and other sources cited by Reuters.

The move would end the diplomatic status of British personnel based in Jerusalem after the deadline. Reuters also reported that diplomats working in Ramallah were given seven days to leave and that Britain would no longer be permitted to train Palestinian security personnel.

The order follows sanctions imposed by Britain, France and Canada connected to Israeli settlements. It marks a sharp deterioration in diplomatic relations and could affect Britain’s long-standing work with Palestinians in Jerusalem and the West Bank.

Because the instructions and timelines were reported through officials and sources, implementation details may still change. Britain’s government had not announced a reversal in the initial account. The closure order is therefore a developing diplomatic action, with practical questions remaining about consular services, staffing and how British engagement with Palestinian institutions will continue.
dek: The order gives the British mission 30 days to close and follows settlement-related sanctions imposed by Britain, France and Canada.
headline: Israel orders Britain to close East Jerusalem consulate

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Large companies and public bodies are putting critical digital infrastructure under more direct board-level scrutiny as cyber threats, export controls and geopolitical conflict expose technology dependencies, a Capgemini survey found.

The survey covered executives at 1,300 large organizations in 11 countries, Reuters reported. Respondents increasingly treated cloud services, data, artificial-intelligence models and other digital systems like energy supplies or physical supply chains that require risk assessments and contingency plans.

Nearly half said replacing a critical provider would take between three months and a year. More than a third expected the switch to take longer than a year, suggesting that contractual access alone does not guarantee a quick recovery when a major vendor becomes unavailable.

The response is not necessarily a wholesale shift away from established providers. Organizations are focusing on whether important workloads can move, whether proprietary assets remain under their control and whether alternate suppliers are practical. That emphasis turns technical resilience into a governance and business-continuity issue, not solely an information-technology concern.
dek: A survey of 1,300 organizations found that replacing a critical provider could take months or longer, pushing resilience into board discussions.
headline: Boards elevate digital-infrastructure resilience as risks grow

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A University Orthopedics surgeon has performed Rhode Island’s first use of a newer thumb-joint replacement implant, offering another surgical option for selected patients with advanced arthritis.

Dr. Joseph Gil performed the procedure for patient LuAnn Pratas, who had stage-three arthritis, WJAR reported. The implant has been used in Europe for more than a decade and replaces the damaged thumb joint with a prosthesis rather than relying on the traditional operation described in the report.

WJAR said the device received U.S. Food and Drug Administration premarket approval for an observational period and is currently covered by Medicare. Gil said two additional patients were being lined up for the procedure.

The first-in-state case is an early adoption milestone, not proof that the implant is appropriate for every patient or superior in all circumstances. Coverage outside Medicare may remain limited while evidence is collected. People considering surgery should discuss established alternatives, implant risks, rehabilitation needs and insurance authorization with a qualified hand specialist.
dek: University Orthopedics used a prosthetic implant already established in Europe for a Rhode Island patient with advanced thumb arthritis.
headline: Rhode Island surgeon performs state’s first new thumb-joint replacement

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Brent crude briefly rose above $100 a barrel Wednesday as the conflict in the Middle East intensified concerns about oil production and shipping routes.

Reuters reported that Brent reached $100.19 during trading before easing to $99.93. U.S. West Texas Intermediate was reported at $94.52. The move put Brent above $100 for the first time since July 24.

Those figures were snapshots from Wednesday’s session, not live prices, and they can change quickly. Traders were assessing risks to supply infrastructure and traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy exports.

The threshold matters because sustained crude gains can raise fuel and transportation costs and complicate the inflation outlook. A brief move above $100 does not establish where oil will close or remain. Investors and consumers should check current market data for later prices and watch confirmed shipping, production and inventory updates rather than treating conflict headlines alone as proof of a lasting shortage.
dek: Reuters reported Brent touched $100.19 before easing, crossing the threshold for the first time since July 24 amid Middle East supply concerns.
headline: Brent crude breaks above $100 as supply fears deepen

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The cost of moving oil through the Strait of Hormuz has climbed into a range of $10 million to $20 million for some voyages after the Iran war, an Emirates National Oil Company executive said Wednesday.

ENOC director Paul Bradshaw told the APPEC conference that cargo insurance could reach 5% to 6% of a shipment’s value, potentially adding about $10 million. Additional war-risk premiums that were previously zero can now run as high as 10%, Reuters reported.

Bradshaw said some market participants were choosing to go without insurance, while a limited number of shipowners were willing to accept the safety risk. Some national oil companies have taken greater control of their own shipping operations.

The figures are an industry executive’s reported estimates, not a universal tariff for every vessel. Actual costs vary by cargo, route, insurer and risk assessment. Even so, the increase shows how conflict can affect energy markets without an immediate change in production: higher insurance, longer routes and fewer willing ships can tighten vessel availability and raise delivered costs.
dek: An ENOC executive said insurance and war-risk premiums can push some voyage costs into an eight-figure range through the key oil route.
headline: Hormuz oil-transit costs surge as insurers price war risk

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Ben Shelton knocked defending champion Carlos Alcaraz out of the U.S. Open early Wednesday, winning a five-set quarterfinal that produced the latest finish in tournament history.
Shelton prevailed 6-7(5), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6(10-7). The match began at 11:05 p.m. Tuesday and ended at 3:33 a.m. after four hours and 28 minutes, Reuters reported.
The result sends Shelton into an all-American semifinal against Frances Tiafoe. It also ended Alcaraz’s 13-match unbeaten record against American opponents at Grand Slam tournaments.

The timing became part of the story as players and spectators remained at Arthur Ashe Stadium well into the morning. Shelton had to recover after dropping the opening tiebreak and again after Alcaraz forced a deciding set. The final tiebreak decided a match in which momentum swung repeatedly, leaving an American guaranteed a place in the men’s final. The United States has not produced a men’s Grand Slam singles champion since Andy Roddick in 2003.
dek: Shelton beat the defending champion in five sets at 3:33 a.m., setting up an all-American semifinal against Frances Tiafoe.
headline: Ben Shelton stuns Carlos Alcaraz in latest U.S. Open finish

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Frances Tiafoe reached the U.S. Open semifinals for the third time after rallying from two sets and a break down against fellow American Alex Michelsen.
The 11th seed won 5-7, 3-6, 7-5, 6-3, 7-6(6) on Tuesday at Arthur Ashe Stadium, Reuters reported. Michelsen served for the match in the third set, but Tiafoe broke back and shifted the momentum.
The victory set up an all-American semifinal against Ben Shelton, who later defeated defending champion Carlos Alcaraz. It guarantees a U.S. player a place in the men’s final.

Tiafoe also reached the tournament’s semifinals in 2022 and 2024. His latest run keeps alive the effort to end a long drought in American men’s major singles tennis: Andy Roddick remains the last U.S. man to win a Grand Slam title, at the 2003 U.S. Open. The semifinal matchup is now fixed, but its schedule and any later tournament details should be confirmed with organizers.
dek: The American recovered from two sets and a break down to beat Alex Michelsen and earn a semifinal meeting with Ben Shelton.
headline: Frances Tiafoe completes comeback to reach U.S. Open semifinals

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Catholic Medical Center has awarded Granite United Way a $25,000 grant aimed at supporting Manchester children, new mothers and first responders through several community programs.

The hospital said the funding will help provide back-to-school resources and supplies, infant-safety education and kits for new mothers and babies. It also will support mental-health training designed for emergency personnel who routinely encounter traumatic events.

According to the hospital, the grant will fund multiple day-long training sessions for nearly 100 first responders and expand outreach intended to reach more than 100 families. The award is part of a broader $2 million community commitment by CMC parent HCA Healthcare.

The projects address different needs but share an early-intervention focus: giving families practical supplies at vulnerable moments and helping responders recognize and manage the strain of emergency work. Because the announcement describes planned services, the next useful measures will be participation, delivery of the promised resources and whether the programs continue after this grant period.
dek: A $25,000 grant to Granite United Way will fund school resources, infant-safety supplies and mental-health training for first responders.
headline: Catholic Medical Center grant expands Manchester family and first-responder support

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Manchester completed its first month without a suspected overdose fatality since 2015, according to a report from American Medical Response announced by the city.

The city described the result as the first such month in 140 months. Officials credited coordinated work by emergency medical crews, police, firefighters, public-health teams, treatment providers and recovery organizations, while emphasizing that the opioid crisis remains an active threat.

The milestone concerns suspected overdose deaths reported for the month, not a declaration that the crisis is over or that all cases have completed final review. A single month also does not establish a lasting trend. Even so, the absence of a suspected fatality marks a notable break from more than a decade of continuous loss.

Manchester said continued prevention, rapid response and recovery support remain necessary. The city directed people seeking substance-use treatment to New Hampshire’s Doorway program through 211 and reminded residents to call 911 for a suspected overdose. Future monthly data will show whether the improvement is sustained.
dek: American Medical Response reported that Manchester completed its first month in 140 months without a suspected overdose fatality.
headline: Manchester records first month without a suspected overdose death since 2015

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Orange Line service between Forest Hills and Back Bay will be suspended for five consecutive days beginning Thursday, September 10, as work continues on the Ruggles Station Improvements Project.

The closure runs through Monday, September 14. Free, accessible shuttle buses will stop between Forest Hills and Back Bay, but riders should expect crowding and longer trips. Boston’s advisory says a Forest Hills rider heading to Downtown Crossing should budget at least 30 extra minutes.

Commuter Rail trips between Forest Hills, Ruggles, Back Bay and South Station will be fare-free during the shutdown. The trip from Forest Hills to Back Bay takes about 10 minutes, although rail schedules may make that alternative more practical for some trips than others.

All replacement buses are accessible, but weekday service may include lift-equipped coach buses; weekend shuttles will use low-floor, ramp-equipped vehicles. Riders should check current MBTA alerts before leaving because the city’s closure calendar covers planned diversions rather than live conditions. Regular Orange Line service north of Back Bay is expected to continue.
dek: Free shuttle buses and fare-free Commuter Rail service will cover the September 10–14 closure for work at Ruggles Station.
headline: Five-day Orange Line shutdown starts Thursday between Forest Hills and Back Bay

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Boston Logan International Airport is expected to add TSA PreCheck E-gates using facial-comparison technology, along with 3D scanners designed to inspect bags without requiring travelers to unpack them manually.

TSA Administrator David Cummins told CBS News Boston that PreCheck travelers would be able to keep a driver’s license and boarding pass in their pocket while moving through the gate. The bag scanners would create a three-dimensional view that lets screeners digitally inspect contents.

Travelers outside PreCheck are also expected to see walk-through body-scanning technology that does not require passengers to raise their hands. The report did not provide a firm installation date, so travelers should not assume the new process is available on a particular trip until Logan or TSA confirms it.

A separate program allowing some PreCheck members without tickets to accompany arriving or departing travelers is operating at 13 airports. Logan has not joined that program; an airport spokesperson said officials are monitoring it. That distinction matters because the planned screening equipment and visitor-access policy are separate changes.
dek: TSA says facial-comparison gates and 3D bag scanners are coming to Logan, while a separate visitor-access program remains under review.
headline: Logan Airport plans E-gates and scanners that digitally unpack bags

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Rhode Island’s Office of the Child Advocate says the state’s child-protection system needs immediate changes after a review identified persistent weaknesses in screening, staffing and prevention services.

The review covered 30 fatalities and 11 near-fatalities involving children with current or prior Department of Children, Youth and Families contact. Child Advocate Katelyn Medeiros said reviewers found cases that should have been accepted for investigation but were screened out, along with families who sought help but were not connected to prevention services.

The report contains 76 recommendations spanning Child Protective Services practices, the Support and Response Unit, oversight and longer-term system improvements. Investigators also found caseloads above national best-practice levels and delays in responding to families within the department’s own timelines.

Medeiros said staffing is part of the problem but not the only answer; policy, law, regulation and internal systems also need better alignment. The findings describe a reform agenda rather than completed changes. Accountability will depend on which recommendations DCYF accepts, the timeline for implementation and whether lawmakers or administrators provide the necessary authority and resources.
dek: A review of 30 fatalities and 11 near-fatalities identified inconsistent screening, high caseloads and missed opportunities to connect families with help.
headline: Rhode Island child advocate calls for immediate child-protection changes

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Two raccoons found in populated Warwick neighborhoods tested positive for rabies, bringing Rhode Island’s 2026 total to 34 confirmed rabid animals, the Department of Health said.

One raccoon was found near Walter Street and the other near Duncan Road. Three adults and two dogs connected to the Walter Street area received treatment, while another dog was treated after a possible exposure near Duncan Road.

The statewide count already exceeds the average of 24 rabid animals reported annually from 2021 through 2025. Health officials said 43 people have received treatment after exposure this year. The confirmed animals include 20 raccoons, 10 bats, one cat, one coyote, one skunk and one woodchuck.

RIDOH advises residents not to approach or feed wild or free-roaming animals and to keep dogs, cats and ferrets current on rabies vaccinations. Anyone who may have had direct contact with either raccoon should contact RIDOH promptly for an exposure assessment. Possible pet exposures should be reported to the department, local animal control and a veterinarian.
dek: The state’s 2026 total already exceeds the recent annual average, and health officials are urging residents to avoid contact with wildlife.
headline: Rhode Island rabies count reaches 34 after two Warwick raccoons test positive

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Several merchant vessels in the northern Gulf and Gulf of Oman were hit by disabling fires during overnight military activity, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported Wednesday.

The British navy-affiliated agency said it could not initially confirm casualties or environmental damage. In a separate incident about 24 nautical miles from Port Rashid in the United Arab Emirates, UKMTO reported a vessel listing at anchor, possibly after taking on water following an attack by an unknown projectile.

The incidents came after U.S. Central Command said it destroyed five Iranian crude tankers following attempted missile attacks on a U.S. Navy warship. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards then claimed attacks on two U.S. vessels and eight oil tankers. Those claims remained attributed statements in the early reporting, not independently confirmed findings.

The situation is developing, and basic facts may change as crews, ship operators and maritime authorities report damage. Confirmed casualty numbers, pollution effects, vessel identities and consequences for commercial traffic were not available in the initial account. Shipping advisories and official notices will be the key sources for operational updates.
dek: A British maritime agency reported several ships disabled during overnight military activity, with casualties and environmental effects not yet confirmed.
headline: Merchant vessels disabled by fires in Gulf and Gulf of Oman

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Indonesia produced the world’s highest fire-related carbon dioxide emissions during the first week of September as wildfires burned through drought-stricken forest and peatland on Borneo and Sumatra.

Fire Emissions Watch, developed by the European Union’s Copernicus climate service, estimated 19.7 million metric tons from September 1 through September 7. That was more than one-third of the global total and 273% above Indonesia’s seasonal average, though below the same week in the severe 2015 fire year.

Authorities described the current season as the country’s most intense in 11 years. More than 13,000 hotspots were recorded from August 1 through September 8. In Pontianak, West Kalimantan, the air-quality index reached 394 on Wednesday; readings above 300 are considered hazardous.

The emergency remains developing because El Niño-driven heat and drought can sustain fires into October. Satellite estimates may also miss low-temperature or underground peat fires. Later field assessments will be needed to measure burned area, health effects and cross-border haze, while current air-quality readings can vary by place and hour.
dek: Satellite-based estimates put Indonesia’s fire emissions at 19.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide from September 1–7 as drought fuels a severe season.
headline: Indonesia wildfire emissions rise to world’s highest

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Booking Holdings lost its challenge to the European Union’s veto of its €1.63 billion acquisition of flight-booking company ETraveli, leaving the blocked technology deal intact.

The General Court in Luxembourg sided with the European Commission, which rejected the transaction in 2023. Judges said the purchase would have strengthened Booking’s already dominant position in the online travel-agency market for hotels.

Regulators argued that adding ETraveli’s flight-booking services could create a broader travel ecosystem that rivals would struggle to match. Booking’s brands include Booking.com, Rentalcars, Priceline and Agoda. ETraveli, owned by CVC Capital Partners, operates Gotogate, Mytrip and the airline-content service TripStack.

The ruling underscores Europe’s tougher scrutiny of technology acquisitions that may reinforce an incumbent’s position rather than simply add a direct competitor. It does not necessarily end the case: Booking can appeal on points of law to the Court of Justice of the European Union. Until any successful appeal, the Commission’s prohibition remains in force.
dek: Europe’s second-highest court backed regulators who said the €1.63 billion deal would strengthen Booking’s dominant online-travel position.
headline: EU court upholds veto of Booking’s ETraveli acquisition

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Defense startup Covenant has unveiled Anthem, a ground-launched cruise missile the company says can be produced faster and at a lower price than many established long-range weapons.

The company told Reuters that Anthem carries a payload exceeding 200 kilograms and has completed more than 200 test flights over the past year. Covenant is targeting a mid-six-figure unit price once production reaches scale and says it has booked about $150 million in orders.

Founded in 2024, Covenant has raised more than $250 million and employs over 200 people in the United States, Germany and Israel. Its new Dallas plant is designed for annual capacity of 5,000 missiles; a similarly sized German facility has the same target, while an Israeli site is planned for 2,000.

Those figures are company plans, not completed production. New defense manufacturers often face certification, contracting and supply-chain obstacles when moving from tests to high-volume delivery. Covenant expects an international customer to begin receiving German-built units late this year and U.S. Army deliveries in 2027.
dek: The startup says its Anthem missile has completed more than 200 test flights and is backed by about $150 million in orders.
headline: Covenant unveils lower-cost cruise missile designed for mass production

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Rising Japanese government-bond yields may encourage banks, insurers and other domestic institutions to keep more investment in Japan, Fitch Ratings said Wednesday.

Japan’s benchmark 10-year yield reached 3% last week for the first time since September 1996, reflecting concerns about inflation, public finances and the pace of Bank of Japan tightening. Fitch expects policy rates to rise faster than market consensus in 2026 and 2027.

Higher domestic returns reduce the incentive to seek yield overseas. Fitch said Japanese megabanks are cautiously rebuilding government-bond holdings, while life insurers are selling lower-coupon securities and reinvesting in bonds with higher coupons. It saw no sign that the roughly $2 trillion Government Pension Investment Fund had changed its allocation.

Reuters reported that markets had priced in a near certainty of a rise in the central bank’s key rate to 1.25% next week, but that was a market snapshot rather than a confirmed decision. Fitch said it did not expect a fire sale of Japanese government bonds even if yields continue rising.
dek: Higher local returns are prompting banks and insurers to reassess domestic debt as Japan’s benchmark 10-year yield reaches a three-decade high.
headline: Rising Japanese bond yields could keep more investment at home, Fitch says

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The Indian rupee recovered from a session low Wednesday after traders said the Reserve Bank of India likely entered the currency market to slow a decline driven by higher oil prices and dollar outflows.

Reuters reported that the rupee fell to 95.2250 per U.S. dollar before recovering to 95.07 following the suspected intervention. The central bank did not confirm the action in the initial account, so the explanation remains based on traders’ assessment of market activity.

India is a major oil importer, making its currency particularly sensitive when crude prices rise because importers need more dollars to pay energy bills. Portfolio outflows can add to that demand and increase depreciation pressure.

The quoted exchange rates were intraday snapshots from September 9, not live prices, and may have changed after publication. The move shows the challenge facing the RBI: intervention can reduce abrupt volatility, but sustained oil costs and capital flows can continue to influence the currency. Later official data may clarify the scale of any central-bank operation.
dek: Traders said the Reserve Bank of India likely intervened after rising oil costs and dollar outflows pushed the currency to a session low.
headline: Indian rupee recovers after reported central-bank support

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: New York City has released more than 170,000 pages of records documenting its response to the September 11 attacks and the years that followed, including files tied to health and air-quality concerns.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the disclosure Tuesday, September 8. Reuters reported that the release accompanies settlements in two lawsuits seeking access to post-9/11 records. The city’s action makes a large body of material available ahead of the attacks’ 25th anniversary.

The records could help survivors, families, researchers and journalists trace what officials knew, how agencies communicated and how environmental and health concerns were handled. Their volume also means meaningful review will take time; releasing pages does not by itself establish what individual documents show.

Questions about exposure and long-term illness have remained central to the public record of the disaster and cleanup. The disclosure creates an opportunity for independent examination, but conclusions should be tied to specific documents and supporting evidence. Additional reporting may identify gaps, duplicated material or records that require context from the agencies that created them.
dek: The disclosure documents the city’s response to the attacks and aftermath and resolves two lawsuits seeking access to health and air-quality files.
headline: New York City releases 170,000 pages of post-9/11 health and air records

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Jessica Pegula reached the U.S. Open semifinals for a third consecutive year after rallying from a set down to defeat fellow American Emma Navarro.

Pegula won 3-6, 6-4, 6-3 Tuesday at Arthur Ashe Stadium. The 32-year-old recovered from an error-filled opening set, improved enough to level the match and used an extra service break to control the deciding set.

The victory was Pegula’s fifth in a row over Navarro, including their meeting at the Cincinnati Open last month. It also marked Pegula’s 50th win of the season, making her the first player on the women’s tour to reach that total in 2026.

Pegula will next face two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka in a rematch of the 2024 U.S. Open final. Reaching the final would require Pegula to reverse that previous result against the world’s top-ranked player. Match timing and later tournament details remain subject to the official U.S. Open schedule.
dek: Pegula rallied past Emma Navarro in three sets to earn a semifinal rematch with two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka.
headline: Jessica Pegula reaches third straight U.S. Open semifinal

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: New Hampshire’s statewide average for regular gasoline reached about $4.19 a gallon on Wednesday, adding another expense for households and businesses entering the fall travel season.

AAA’s September 9 snapshot listed regular gas at $4.1852, compared with $4.1622 a day earlier, $4.0948 a week earlier and $3.0952 one year ago. That makes the year-over-year increase roughly $1.09 a gallon. The national average in the same snapshot was about $4.22.

Prices varied modestly around the state. AAA showed Manchester averaging about $4.17 for regular, while the Portsmouth-Rochester area averaged about $4.19. Diesel was substantially higher, with the statewide average near $5.86 a gallon.

The figures are dated daily averages published by AAA, not live pump quotes, and prices at individual stations can differ. The comparison nevertheless shows how sharply fuel costs have changed over 12 months. Drivers may want to compare local prices before filling up, while transportation-dependent employers and service providers face continuing pressure from higher fuel expenses.
dek: AAA’s September 9 snapshot put regular gasoline at $4.185 a gallon statewide, up about $1.09 from a year earlier.
headline: New Hampshire regular gas averages $4.19 as yearly increase tops a dollar

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Files associated with the New Hampshire Supreme Court were accessed during a cybersecurity incident involving C-Track, a case-management platform used by courts in multiple jurisdictions.

NHPR reported that the state Judicial Branch reviewed the affected material in mid-August and found that names and addresses of people connected to cases filed from 2002 through 2015 had been accessed. The branch said it had not identified exposed Social Security numbers, driver’s-license numbers, birth dates, medical details or health-insurance information in the New Hampshire files.

West Publishing, which operates C-Track, discovered the unauthorized activity on June 30. Its investigation found that an outside party obtained certain files in March. Court systems in 11 states, the U.S. Virgin Islands and Canada were included in the broader incident.

New Hampshire’s Superior and Circuit courts do not use C-Track, limiting the state exposure identified so far to Supreme Court data. The platform continued operating, according to notices about the breach. People whose names appeared in older cases should rely on direct notices or official updates before assuming their sensitive information was involved.
dek: A review found names and addresses in 2002–2015 case files were accessed, while the Judicial Branch said it had not identified exposed sensitive identifiers.
headline: New Hampshire Supreme Court files were accessed in multi-state C-Track breach

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles plans to hold its 2026 annual low-number license-plate lottery drawing Wednesday afternoon, giving applicants a chance to watch the selection process online.

The RMV said the drawing will begin at 2:30 p.m. on September 9 and will be broadcast through Vimeo. The event follows the application period for plates that are sought because of their short or distinctive combinations.
